question: Abdullah casts [Telemin Performance] targeting Nico. In response, Nico casts [Veil of Summer]. Abdullah responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Both Veil of Summer spells resolve before Telemin Performance does (the stack resolves last-in, first-out), so Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first, then Nico's Veil of Summer, and only after that does Telemin Performance try to resolve against Nico. Here's exactly what each spell does, and where the provided rules run out.

Stack order: Abdullah casts Telemin Performance targeting Nico (bottom of stack). Nico responds with Veil of Summer (middle). Abdullah responds with a second Veil of Summer (top). A cast spell "becomes the topmost object on the stack" and "remains on the stack until it resolves" [601.2a], which is why the most recently cast spell — Abdullah's Veil of Summer — resolves first.

1. Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves. Per Veil of Summer's text, it checks "if an opponent has cast a blue or black spell this turn." Abdullah's opponent is Nico, and Nico's only spell this turn (Veil of Summer) is green, so Abdullah does not draw a card. The other two effects still happen unconditionally: "Spells you control can't be countered this turn" (this now protects Telemin Performance, still on the stack, from being countered for the rest of the turn) and "You and permanents you control gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn," so Abdullah gains hexproof from blue/black [Veil of Summer]. Note that Veil of Summer "has no effect until it resolves" [Veil of Summer ruling #1], so none of this happened while it was sitting on the stack.

2. Nico's Veil of Summer resolves next. Now Nico's opponent is Abdullah, who did cast a blue spell this turn (Telemin Performance), so Nico draws a card — only one card, even though only one qualifying spell was cast [Veil of Summer ruling #0]. Nico's spells also can't be countered this turn (moot, since Nico has no other spell on the stack), and Nico and Nico's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn [Veil of Summer].

3. Finally, Telemin Performance tries to resolve, still targeting Nico, who by now has hexproof from blue (and Telemin Performance is a blue sorcery). Here the provided rules stop short of a full answer: they tell us hexproof means Nico "can't be the target[] of blue... spells... opponents control" going forward [Veil of Summer], but none of the rules given to me state whether a spell already legally targeting a player is rechecked for target legality at resolution and fails if the target has since become illegal. That specific rule (the general target-legality check performed when a spell resolves) is not among the rules provided here, so I can't confirm from this rule set whether Telemin Performance fizzles against Nico or still goes through. I don't want to guess at that mechanic without a supporting rule.

What I can say for certain: Abdullah's Veil of Summer does not net a card draw, gives Abdullah hexproof from blue/black and protects Abdullah's spells (including Telemin Performance) from being countered this turn; Nico's Veil of Summer nets Nico one card draw and gives Nico hexproof from blue/black. Whether that hexproof stops the already-targeting Telemin Performance is the one piece this rule set doesn't settle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first. Then Nico's resolves and draws them a card. Then Telemin Performance tries to resolve and fails, since it has an illegal target.

(Abdullah's Veil of Summer didn't accomplish anything useful.)
judge_reason: The candidate declines to rule whether Telemin Performance fizzles after both Veils resolve, whereas the reference states it fails to resolve due to Nico having gained hexproof, so the final conclusions differ.

question: Athena controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nicholas flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Athena's turn. Can Nicholas activate its abilities this turn?
answer:
Yes. Nicholas can activate one loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn, at instant speed, because The Wandering Emperor's own text overrides the normal timing restriction — and Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability doesn't stop him, since that ability only restricts casting spells, not activating loyalty abilities.

Normally, loyalty abilities (rule 606.1, 606.2) can only be activated "any time [the controller] has priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn" (rules 606.3, 209.2). Since Nicholas flashed The Wandering Emperor in during Athena's turn, this turn isn't a main phase of Nicholas's own turn, so that default rule wouldn't normally let him activate anything until his next turn.

However, The Wandering Emperor's printed ability states: "As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant." This is card text that specifically overrides the general timing restriction of rule 606.3/209.2 (card text beats a general rule it contradicts). Because instants can be cast on any player's turn, this permission lets Nicholas activate a loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor right away on Athena's turn, as long as he otherwise has priority (rule 117.1b) — for example, in response to something, or whenever priority passes to him.

Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability ("Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery") restricts Nicholas's ability to *cast spells*, not his ability to *activate abilities*. Activating a loyalty ability is not casting a spell, so this restriction simply does not apply here. The Teferi, Time Raveler ruling about "precedence" only concerns situations where an effect tries to let an opponent cast a spell as though it had flash (i.e., actual spellcasting) — it's not about activating a permanent's abilities, so it doesn't extend to block The Wandering Emperor's loyalty-ability permission.

One caveat: per The Wandering Emperor's own ruling, Nicholas may still only activate one of her loyalty abilities during the turn she entered the battlefield (consistent with the "no player has previously activated a loyalty ability of that permanent that turn" restriction in rule 606.3/209.2). So he gets exactly one activation this turn, but he can do it at instant speed rather than waiting for his own main phase.

This answer assumes Nicholas is an opponent of Athena in a two-player game; the rules given are all framed for a single active player's main phase and don't specify anything different for a multiplayer table beyond that any player with priority may act, so the same reasoning would apply in a multiplayer game as well.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nicholas cannot cast The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn due to Teferi, Time Raveler's effect.
judge_reason: The candidate allows activating The Wandering Emperor's loyalty ability after it was flashed in, whereas the reference says casting it on Athena's turn is prevented by Teferi, so the conclusions conflict.

question: Ariel controls [Rest in Peace] and targets Nataly's [Dauthi Voidwalker] with [Lightning Bolt]. What happens to each card?
answer:
Both Lightning Bolt and Dauthi Voidwalker end up in exile, not in any graveyard — but for different reasons tied to Rest in Peace, not to Dauthi Voidwalker's own ability.

What happens to Dauthi Voidwalker: Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Dauthi Voidwalker (a 3/2), which is lethal damage. Under rule [704.5g], a creature with lethal damage marked on it "has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed" as a state-based action, and this destruction event is normally what sends it to the graveyard, satisfying the definition of "dies" in [700.4] (put into a graveyard from the battlefield). However, Rest in Peace's ability — "If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead" — is a replacement effect ([614.1]) that intercepts this event and sends Dauthi Voidwalker to exile instead of to Nataly's graveyard.

Importantly, Dauthi Voidwalker's own ability ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it") does NOT apply to itself here: Dauthi Voidwalker is owned/controlled by Nataly, and it would be going to Nataly's own graveyard, not "an opponent's" graveyard from Nataly's perspective (its controller). So the only applicable replacement effect is Ariel's Rest in Peace, and no APNAP choice ([101.4], [616.1f]) is even needed since just one effect applies — Dauthi Voidwalker is simply exiled with no void counter, and no "dies" trigger occurs because it never reaches a graveyard.

What happens to Lightning Bolt: after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving, it would normally be put into Ariel's graveyard as a used instant. Rest in Peace's text explicitly covers "a card or token" being put into a graveyard "from anywhere," which includes spells going to the graveyard after resolving — this is confirmed by Rest in Peace's own ruling that even a spell destroying Rest in Peace itself still gets exiled afterward instead of hitting the graveyard [Rest in Peace ruling #1]. So Lightning Bolt is exiled instead of going to Ariel's graveyard.

Note on card text overriding general rules: Rest in Peace's printed replacement effect overrides the normal graveyard-bound outcome that rules [704.5g] and [700.4] would otherwise produce, and it takes priority over Dauthi Voidwalker's ability simply because Dauthi Voidwalker's ability doesn't apply to this particular event at all (it only affects opponents' cards from its controller's point of view). This analysis holds the same whether the game has two players or more, since Dauthi Voidwalker's ability is defined relative to its own controller regardless of table size, and only one replacement effect (Rest in Peace) is actually competing for this event.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Ariel chooses whether Lightning Bolt goes to exile with or without a counter.

There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Lightning Bolt going to the graveyard with it going to exile, so its controller gets to choose which to apply.

Then state-based actions are checked and Dauthi Voidwalker is put into exile.
judge_reason: The candidate denies that Dauthi Voidwalker's replacement ability can apply to Lightning Bolt (and omits the controller's choice), while the reference says both replacement effects apply to the Bolt so its controller chooses whether it is exiled with a void counter.

question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
answer:
No, Arjun cannot activate Molten-Tail Masticore's first activated ability. That ability costs "{4}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: This creature deals 4 damage to any target," and exiling a creature card from the graveyard is part of the activation cost. Under rule 118.3, a player can't pay a cost without having the necessary resources to pay it fully — since Arjun's graveyard has no cards at all, there is no creature card available to exile, so this cost cannot be paid, and the ability can't legally be activated (rule 602.5 confirms a player can't even begin to activate an ability that's prohibited/impossible to pay for). Thermopod's own abilities (its {S} haste ability and its 'Sacrifice a creature: Add {R}' mana ability) don't change this — they could help produce mana or fill the graveyard with a non-creature card via sacrifice, but sacrificing Thermopod itself would put a creature card in the graveyard, which isn't what's happening here since Arjun currently has zero cards in the graveyard when the question is posed. As stated, with an empty graveyard, the additional cost simply cannot be met.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Yes. Arjun first puts the ability onto the stack, after which it won't matter if Molten-Tail Masticore is on the battlefield anymore. Arjun then has a chance to activate mana abilities, at which point they can sacrifice Molten-Tail Masticore. Then Arjun pays the cost of the spell, exiling Molten-Tail Masticore from their graveyard.
judge_reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—saying the activation is illegal because the exile-from-graveyard cost can't be paid with an empty graveyard, whereas the reference says the activation is legal.

question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
answer:
Alivia can only cast Road, the instant half of Road // Ruin - not Ruin, the sorcery/aftermath half. Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability reads 'you may cast target instant card from your graveyard without paying its mana cost,' so it can only target and cast a card using its instant characteristics. While Road // Ruin sits in the graveyard (not on the stack), it has the combined characteristics of both halves - it is simultaneously an instant card and a sorcery card, per the card's own ruling (Road // Ruin ruling #3: 'While not on the stack, the characteristics of a split card are the combination of its two halves... it is both an instant card and a sorcery card'). That combined status makes it a legal target for Torrential Gearhulk's ability. However, per rule 601.3e, when an effect lets you cast a spell using only a subset of its characteristics (here, 'instant card'), only the alternative/qualifying characteristics are used to determine what can legally be cast - the rule's own Melek, Izzet Paragon example shows that an effect restricted to casting instants can only cast the instant-type option of a card with mixed characteristics, not the other side. Applying that logic here, Torrential Gearhulk's ability lets Alivia cast only the Road face (the instant), not the Ruin face (a sorcery). This also lines up with Road // Ruin ruling #0, which confirms that when you cast a split card you put only the half you're casting onto the stack, with the other half's characteristics ignored - so Alivia would be casting Road alone, as an instant spell, without paying its mana cost. Separately, Ruin could never be cast this way regardless, since Ruin has aftermath and can normally only be cast from the graveyard as its own sorcery spell (Road // Ruin ruling #5 notes that if another effect lets you cast a split card with aftermath from a zone other than the graveyard, you can't cast the aftermath half at all) - but here the deciding factor is simply that Torrential Gearhulk's ability only ever authorizes casting the instant portion. Finally, per Torrential Gearhulk ruling #0, this casting happens immediately as part of the ability's resolution - Alivia cannot hold Road to cast it later in the turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Either side. Torrential Gearhulk has a targeting restriction that requires Alivia to select an instant in their graveyard. Split cards have the type of both sides simultaneously. Therefore Road // Ruin is both an instant and a sorcery card and satisfies the targeting restriction on Torrential Gearhulk. When Alivia goes to cast Road // Ruin, nothing cares about which half is cast, so either is legal.
judge_reason: The reference says either half may be cast, while the candidate insists only the instant half (Road) can be cast, so they reach different conclusions.

question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
answer:
Autumn's attempt to cast Insurrection is illegal, so it never actually gets cast, and Tempted by the Oriq stays on the stack to resolve normally targeting the Soldier tokens.

Here's why: Insurrection is a sorcery, and sorceries can normally only be cast when a player could cast a sorcery — with an object (Tempted by the Oriq) already on the stack, Autumn does not otherwise have permission to cast it. Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born's Cosmic Awareness ability reads, "As long as an opponent has cast a spell this turn, you may cast spells as though they had flash." The only spell cast this turn so far is Tempted by the Oriq, and Autumn herself cast it — it was not cast by an opponent (Breanna or Case). Because the ability's condition requires an *opponent* to have cast a spell, and that hasn't happened, Cosmic Awareness does not grant Autumn flash permission at this moment. Captain Mar-Vell's printed text is what defines this condition, and it overrides nothing here since no general rule contradicts it — it simply isn't satisfied.

Since Autumn is not legally allowed to cast Insurrection at that time, rule [601.2a] applies: a player must be legally allowed to cast a spell to begin the casting process, and if the requirements can't be met, the casting is illegal and "the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed." So the illegal casting of Insurrection is unwound completely — it goes back to Autumn's hand as if she never attempted to cast it, no mana is paid, and no priority passes for it.

Tempted by the Oriq remains the only spell on the stack, controlled by Autumn. Once players return to that point and pass priority in succession, it will resolve per [608.1]/[117.4], checking at that time under [608.2b] whether Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens are still legal targets (still controlled by those players, mana value 3 or less, etc.) before Autumn gains control of them.

One clarifying note on the multiplayer aspect: this scenario has three players (Autumn, Breanna, Case), so it's a multiplayer game. Nothing here changes because of that under the standard single-stack model — rule [405.2] describes one shared stack where objects are added to the top regardless of how many players there are. If your table is instead using a variant like Grand Melee with multiple simultaneous stacks [807.5b], the specific stack a spell is put on matters (e.g., it would need to match the stack of anything it targets), but that variant isn't indicated here, so this answer assumes the normal single-stack multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Insurrection resolves and Autumn gains control of all the Soldier tokens. Then Tempted by the Oriq begins to resolve, but its targets are now illegal, so it does not resolve and is removed from the stack.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Insurrection cannot be cast and therefore Tempted resolves, which contradicts the reference that Insurrection resolves first giving Autumn control of the tokens and making Tempted's targets illegal.

question: Amara controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nehemiah casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
After Humility resolves, Wayward Angel becomes a black, ability-less 3/3 creature — Angel Horror named "Wayward Angel" with mana cost {4}{W}{W}.

Here's why, working through Magic's layer system (rule 613.1, 613.2c):

1. Wayward Angel's threshold clause ("As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, this creature gets +3/+3, is black, has trample, and has '...sacrifice a creature'") is a static ability, not a characteristic-defining ability, because it only sets characteristics *conditionally* on graveyard count — rule [604.3a] explicitly excludes abilities that "set the values of such characteristics only if certain conditions are met" from being CDAs. That matters because a real CDA can't be stripped by a 'loses all abilities' effect, but a normal granted ability can be [113.12].

2. Because more than seven cards are in Amara's graveyard, threshold is active, so before Humility resolves Wayward Angel's color-setting effect (layer 5) already makes it black — per the Wayward Angel ruling, it is black and not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #0].

3. Humility's static ability "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" is a layer 6 (abilities) and layer 7b (set P/T) effect. Layer 5 (color) is calculated before layer 6 (abilities) in the fixed layer order, so the color already locked in during layer 5 is not retroactively undone when the threshold ability is stripped in layer 6 — this mirrors exactly how the Humility/Opalescence interaction works, where an earlier layer's result (e.g., the layer 4 type-change) survives even though the source permanent loses its abilities in layer 6 [Humility ruling #0][Humility ruling #2][613.2c]. So Wayward Angel remains black.

4. In layer 6, however, Humility (with a later timestamp than Wayward Angel, since Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield when Humility was cast) strips away Wayward Angel's flying, vigilance, and the entire threshold ability itself (trample, the upkeep sacrifice ability, and the ability that would have produced +3/+3). Once the threshold ability is gone, none of its not-yet-applied effects (the +3/+3 boost, which is a layer 7c effect) can occur, since the source ability no longer exists by the time layer 7 is reached. Wayward Angel ends layer 6 with no abilities at all.

5. In layer 7b, Humility's own ability (Humility is not itself a creature here, so it keeps its own ability) sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1, overwriting the printed 4/4 [208.4b].

6. In layer 7c, Muraganda Petroglyphs checks whether Wayward Angel "has no abilities." Since step 4 stripped every ability Wayward Angel had, it now qualifies, and Muraganda Petroglyphs' own ability (which belongs to Muraganda Petroglyphs, not to Wayward Angel, so it doesn't itself grant Wayward Angel an ability — see the Runeclaw Bear/'is red' example in [113.12]) applies +2/+2. Final power/toughness: 1/1 base + 2/+2 = 3/3.

So Wayward Angel is: name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, card type Creature — Angel Horror, color black, no abilities (no flying, vigilance, trample, threshold, or the sacrifice trigger), and power/toughness 3/3.

This conclusion doesn't depend on how many players are in the game — nothing here involves opponent choice, turn order, or other multiplayer-specific rules, so the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game.

One timing note: this assumes Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield with threshold active before Humility was cast (so Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp for layer 6/7 ordering purposes). If Humility had instead entered the battlefield first and Wayward Angel entered afterward, the timestamp order for the layer-6 'loses all abilities' vs. Wayward Angel's own printed abilities could differ, but since Humility's effect is a continuous 'lose all abilities' effect that keeps re-applying to whatever creature is on the battlefield, Wayward Angel would still end up losing its abilities either way — the black color from layer 5 is the one detail sensitive to relative timing, and only applies if threshold's color-setting effect was 'in effect' before layer 6 strips the ability that produces it, which is guaranteed by the fixed layer order regardless of timestamps.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Wayward Angel is a Black, 6/6 creature with no abilities. The rest of its characteristics remain the same as printed on the card. 
Wayward Angel's threshold ability changes both its color, abilities, and P/T. Therefore, it applies in layers 5, 6, and 7 with the appropriate parts applying in their appropriate layers, and the layers are applied in order. Similarly, Humility's effect is applied in layers 6 and 7, as appropriate. 
Applying layers in order:
- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. The effects are then applied in timestamp order with Wayward Angel's ability applying first, since it has an earlier timestamp. So in layer 6, Wayward Angel first gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.", and then loses all abilities to Humility.
- In layer 7, P/T setting effects are applied first, so that Humility first turns Wayward Angel into a 1/1. Then effects modifying P/T are applied, of which there are two: Wayward Angel's own ability that, even though removed, continues to apply and gives it +3/+3, and Muraganda Petroglyphs's ability giving Wayward Angel +2/+2 since it now has no abilities. Wayward Angel's P/T is finally 6/6.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Wayward Angel is a black, ability-less 3/3, while the reference concludes it is a black, ability-less 6/6 — the two reach different final power/toughness rulings due to conflicting layer/ability treatment.

question: Nayeli controls [Trinisphere]. Ainsley casts [Noxious Revival], paying 2 life for the Phyrexian mana. What is the total cost of the Noxious Revival?
answer:
The total cost Ainsley must pay is 2 life (for the {G/P} symbol, which Ainsley chose to pay via life) plus {2} of generic mana added by Trinisphere — i.e., the equivalent of a {2}{G/P} cost, paid as {2} generic mana plus 2 life.

Here's why: Noxious Revival's mana cost is just {G/P}, a single Phyrexian mana symbol. For purposes of determining a spell's total cost, a Phyrexian mana symbol is treated as one unit of the mana component of the cost regardless of how it's ultimately paid (this is the same principle behind rule [202.3g] and [Noxious Revival ruling #1], which count a Phyrexian symbol as 1 toward mana value no matter the payment method). Since Trinisphere's effect triggers on 'each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast' ([Trinisphere ruling #0] confirms you check the mana component of the cost against three mana), and {G/P} amounts to only 1 mana, Trinisphere increases the cost to three mana total. Just as Trinisphere's own text illustrates that a {1}{B} spell becomes {2}{B} (adding generic mana to reach three, while leaving the colored symbol untouched), a {G/P} spell becomes {2}{G/P} — Trinisphere adds {2} generic mana, and the original {G/P} symbol is unaffected in kind.

Under rule [601.2b], the player announces whether to pay 2 life or a colored mana for each Phyrexian symbol before the total cost is finally locked in under [601.2f]; Ainsley announced paying 2 life for the {G/P}. That choice doesn't change how Trinisphere evaluates the mana component of the cost (it's still counted as contributing 1 'mana' to the pre-Trinisphere cost) — it only determines how that symbol is actually paid. So the resulting total cost, once locked in per [601.2f] and [Total Cost], is: 2 life (paid instead of {G} for the Phyrexian symbol) + {2} generic mana (Trinisphere's increase, payable with any color of mana or colorless mana, per Trinisphere's own reminder text and [107.4f]/[106.9] on Phyrexian symbols being colored, one-color-only, not generic).

Note: the spell's mana value remains 1, unaffected by Trinisphere's cost increase or by how the Phyrexian symbol is paid ([Trinisphere ruling #0], [202.3g]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: {3} and 2 life. While casting Noxious Revival, Ainsley chooses whether to pay life or mana for each Phyrexian mana symbol in the cost. Trinisphere is applied afterwards and increases the cost up to the minimum of 3 mana.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes the cost is {2} plus 2 life, whereas the correct ruling is {3} plus 2 life, so the final costs do not match.

question: Amirah controls Azors Gateway with 4 different CMC cards exiled by it. They targets it with [Karn's Touch]. After that resolves, they activates [Azor's Gateway], and transforms it into [Sanctum of the Sun]. What are the characteristics of the new object after it has transformed?
answer:
After Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun transforms, the resulting object is still the same permanent as before (rule [712.18]: transforming does not create a new object), so the continuous effect from Karn's Touch keeps applying to it.

Concretely, the permanent is now:
- The back face, Sanctum of the Sun (a Legendary Land), which untapped and transformed as part of resolving its own ability ("gain 5 life, untap Azor's Gateway, and transform it").
- Still an artifact creature, because Karn's Touch's effect ("Target noncreature artifact becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value until end of turn") was already applied while it was Azor's Gateway, and per rule [712.18] and rule [112.4] that continuous effect keeps applying to the permanent even after it transforms. So Sanctum of the Sun is a Legendary Artifact Land Creature until end of turn.
- Its power and toughness are still defined as "equal to its mana value." Since Sanctum of the Sun has no printed mana cost, its mana value is 0, so as the permanent's mana value changes with the new face, the effect recalculates and the creature is 0/0.
- It retains all its abilities, as Karn's Touch explicitly notes ("It retains its abilities"), so it still has Sanctum of the Sun's ability, "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total," plus whatever base characteristics the land face has (it's colorless, since neither face gives it a color and Karn's Touch does not change color).

Note: the provided rules do not include the state-based action for creatures with 0 toughness, so I can't confirm from the given rules whether a 0/0 creature would then be put into the graveyard — that would require a rule not present in this context.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 Legendary artifact creature land with the ability "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total". The requirement that Azor's Gateway be an artifact is part of the targeting restriction of the spell, after the spell resolves, it creates a continuous effect on the permanent that was targeted (in this case Azor's Gateway) that lasts until end of turn. When a double-faced card transforms it doesn't become a new object, and any effects that applied to it before the transformation will continue to apply afterwards.

question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
answer:
At the beginning of that end step, Nicholas (Paralyze's controller) chooses what Paralyze enchants, and the only legal choices are Onakke Ogre or Ascended Lawmage — Paralyze cannot attach to Cemetery Gate.

Here's why. Sudden Disappearance exiled all nonland permanents Nicholas controlled — that includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze, since Paralyze was a permanent Nicholas controlled (even though it enchanted his own creature). All the exiled cards return to the battlefield simultaneously at the beginning of the next end step, under each card's owner's control. Sudden Disappearance's return effect does not say what Paralyze will be attached to when it comes back, so rule [303.4f] governs: when an Aura enters the battlefield under a player's control by a means other than resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn't specify what it enchants, that player (Nicholas, since Paralyze returns under its owner's control) chooses what it enchants, and must choose a legal object according to Paralyze's enchant ability ('Enchant creature') and any other applicable effects.

Because Onakke Ogre is returning to the battlefield at the same moment via the same effect, it is available as a choice — Nicholas may simply have Paralyze come back attached to his own Onakke Ogre. Alternatively, Paralyze's enchant ability only says 'creature,' with no controller restriction, so any other creature on the battlefield is also eligible. Ascended Lawmage has hexproof, but hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities an opponent controls — the choice a player makes under [303.4f] as an Aura enters the battlefield is not a targeting event, so hexproof does not prevent Nicholas from choosing to enchant Ascended Lawmage with Paralyze.

Cemetery Gate, however, has protection from black printed on it, and Paralyze is a black Aura ({B} cost). Protection's 'can't be enchanted by' component is an 'applicable effect' under [303.4f] that makes Cemetery Gate an illegal object for Paralyze to enchant, so Nicholas cannot choose it.

If Nicholas were to somehow fail to attach Paralyze to any legal creature (there is no reason he would, since two legal choices exist), the state-based action in [704.5m] would send the unattached Aura straight to its owner's graveyard.

This answer assumes there is no other creature relevant to the game state besides these three; if any other creature is present, it would also be a legal target subject to the same protection/hexproof analysis.

question: Alex controls [Rhythm of the Wild], [Grumgully, the Generous], [Renata, Called to the Hunt], and [Hardened Scales]. Alex then casts [Grizzled Outrider]. If they chooses to put a counter on Grizzled Outrider for Rhythm of the Wild, how many +1/+1 counters will it enter with in total?
answer:
Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield with 6 +1/+1 counters on it (assuming Alex chooses the +1/+1 counter option from Rhythm of the Wild's riot rather than haste).

Here's why: Grizzled Outrider (a nontoken, non-Human creature) is affected by three separate "enters the battlefield with an additional/chosen +1/+1 counter" replacement effects that modify how it enters the battlefield: Rhythm of the Wild's riot (Alex chooses the +1/+1 counter option), Grumgully, the Generous's "each other non-Human creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter," and Renata, Called to the Hunt's "each other creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter." None of these conflict with each other (they don't try to modify the exact same instance of the event in mutually exclusive ways), so per rule 614.12b and 616.1f, Alex (as the affected object's controller) chooses the order in which to apply them, and all three end up applying, one after another, until none are left.

Hardened Scales reads "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead." Under rule 614.16, this kind of replacement effect applies not just to a spell or ability's own counter-placement, but also to a counter placement caused by another replacement effect. Since each of the three enter-with-a-counter effects (Rhythm of the Wild, Grumgully, and Renata) independently causes a "1 or more +1/+1 counters would be put on this creature" event, Hardened Scales applies separately to each of those three events, per Hardened Scales ruling #0 ("if a creature you control would enter the battlefield with a number of +1/+1 counters on it, it enters with that many plus one instead") and ruling #1 (the controller chooses the order in which multiple counter-modifying effects apply).

So the math is:
- Rhythm of the Wild's riot counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2
- Grumgully, the Generous's additional counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2
- Renata, Called to the Hunt's additional counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2

Total: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 +1/+1 counters on Grizzled Outrider as it enters the battlefield.

(If Alex had instead chosen haste from Rhythm of the Wild's riot for that instance, only Grumgully's and Renata's counters would apply, each boosted to 2 by Hardened Scales, for a total of 4 counters.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Four. Every card on the battlefield has a replacement effect that modifies how Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield. When applying replacement effects, each effect has a chance to apply once and only once, so even though Alex can choose which order to apply the effects in, Hardened Scales will only get one chance to modify how many counters Grizzled Outrider enters the battlefield with, and will only ever add one additional counter.
judge_reason: The candidate claims 6 counters, but the correct result is 4 because Hardened Scales only applies once to the enter-with-counters replacement (it doesn't add a counter for each separate enter-with effect).

question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
answer:
Minas Tirith enters the battlefield untapped in this scenario. Minas Tirith's ability reads "Minas Tirith enters tapped unless you control a legendary creature." This is a replacement effect that modifies how Minas Tirith enters the battlefield [614.1c]. To determine whether that condition is met, rule [614.12] says you check the characteristics of the entering permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it. Living Plane's static ability, "All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands," is already active on the battlefield before Minas Tirith is played, and per [611.3c] a continuous effect that modifies characteristics of a permanent does so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield, not after a delay. So as Minas Tirith enters, it's already a 1/1 creature - and since Minas Tirith is a Legendary Land, it's a legendary creature the instant it hits the battlefield. That satisfies its own "unless you control a legendary creature" clause, so the enters-tapped replacement doesn't apply, and Minas Tirith enters untapped.

This is different from the situation described in [Minas Tirith ruling #0], where the land requires a legendary creature to already be on the battlefield beforehand, and simultaneous entry of a separate legendary creature doesn't count (that land would enter tapped). Here there's no second permanent entering at the same time - Living Plane is already an established, pre-existing continuous effect on the battlefield, so it's not a case of two objects entering simultaneously; it's a pre-existing effect that shapes what Minas Tirith looks like the instant it becomes a permanent, which is exactly the situation rule [614.12] is written to handle. I'm assuming Living Plane was already on the battlefield before Minas Tirith was played (as the question states, "Ayla controls Living Plane and plays Minas Tirith"); if instead Living Plane were being put onto the battlefield at the exact same time as Minas Tirith, that would be a simultaneous-entry case and, per the logic of ruling #0, Minas Tirith would enter tapped instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Tapped. When applying an enters-the-battlefield replacement effect, the game considers the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, so it sees that it would be a creature, but it doesn't consider the permanent to actually be on the battlefield yet. Effectively, a legendary creature is entering the battlefield.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Minas Tirith enters untapped (arguing Living Plane makes it a legendary creature as it enters), which contradicts the reference ruling that it enters tapped.

question: Andy controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Andy then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands ends up as a Plains and can be tapped only for {W}.

Here's why: Badlands is a nonbasic land whose printed subtype is Swamp Mountain, and it normally has "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" from those two basic land types (Badlands ruling #0). Both Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and Conversion's "All Mountains are Plains" are continuous effects that set a land's subtype (layer 4 type-setting effects). Because Badlands is nonbasic (it never had the basic supertype, and setting its subtype doesn't add or remove supertypes per [305.7]), Magus of the Moon's effect keeps applying to it even after its type changes -- and because Conversion's effect only cares about whatever is currently a Mountain, which set of lands counts as "Mountains" is itself determined by Magus of the Moon's effect. That makes Conversion's effect dependent on Magus of the Moon's effect, so Magus of the Moon's type-setting is applied first, and Conversion's is applied afterward using the result.

Step 1 -- Magus of the Moon: Badlands is nonbasic, so its subtype is set to Mountain. Per [305.7], it loses its old subtypes (Swamp and Mountain) along with the abilities generated by them, and gains the land type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #2; see also ruling #4, which confirms Magus of the Moon's type-changing effect keeps applying even under complications).

Step 2 -- Conversion: Badlands is now literally a Mountain, so Conversion's "All Mountains are Plains" applies to it. Again per [305.7], its subtype is set to Plains, it loses the Mountain type and the {T}: Add {R} ability that came with it, and it gains the Plains type and the intrinsic "{T}: Add {W}" ability (see [305.6] and Conversion ruling #1, which confirms Conversion's effect is a continuous, immediately-applied type change).

Badlands remains a nonbasic land throughout (Conversion doesn't add the basic supertype -- see [113.12] on characteristic-setting effects not granting or removing supertypes), so this reasoning is stable: it stays eligible for Magus of the Moon's "nonbasic lands" clause the whole time, but its actual current type after both effects settle is Plains. Badlands ruling #2 confirms that a land-type-changing effect on a dual land removes the old land types completely, which is what happens twice here.

This is a two-player-neutral interaction (nothing about player count changes how continuous effects layer), so the same result holds whether Andy is in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Note: the specific rule governing how to order two effects that are 'dependent' on each other (i.e., which one is applied first when the timestamp order alone wouldn't give a consistent answer) wasn't included in the rules text I was given, so my ordering above is inferred from how [305.7] describes basic-type-setting effects interacting, plus the card rulings for Magus of the Moon, Conversion, and Badlands, which together describe exactly this chain of type changes.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Only {R}. Both Magus of the Moon and Conversion only apply in layer 4. The effects are applied in timestamp order, resulting in Conversion applying first to make Badlands a Plains, then Magus of the Moon applies making it a Mountain.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Badlands becomes a Plains tapping for {W}, whereas the correct ruling is that it becomes a Mountain and can tap only for {R}.

question: Amy controls a [Trigon of Corruption] enchanted by Neil's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Amy's upkeep, they cast [Aura Graft] to attach the Curse Artifact to [Sungrass Egg]. Which artifact does Amy have the choice to sacrifice as the trigger resolves?

Amy has the choice to sacrifice Sungrass Egg when Curse Artifact's triggered ability resolves — not Trigon of Corruption. Per rule [303.4m], any reference to the "enchanted [object]" refers to whatever object the Aura is currently attached to, and this is a dynamic reference rather than something locked in when the ability triggered (this situation isn't one of the zone-change or unattached-trigger exceptions that would require looking back in time, per [603.10c] and [603.6e]). Because Aura Graft was cast in response to the trigger, it resolves first (spells and abilities resolve in last-in-first-out order), moving Curse Artifact from Trigon of Corruption to Sungrass Egg and giving it a new timestamp under [701.3c]. Once attached to Sungrass Egg, Curse Artifact's ability that "modifies" or references the enchanted permanent now applies to Sungrass Egg instead of Trigon of Corruption, consistent with the general principle in [604.4] that an Aura's effects move with it to whatever it's newly attached to. So when Curse Artifact's upkeep trigger finally resolves, "enchanted artifact" is read as Sungrass Egg, and Amy's choice is whether to sacrifice Sungrass Egg (not Trigon of Corruption) to avoid the 2 damage. Note: the player who takes the damage/must sacrifice ("that player") was fixed at the moment the ability triggered as the controller of the then-enchanted Trigon of Corruption — that was Amy, so Amy remains the player facing the choice; it's only the identity of the artifact referenced by "that artifact" that updates to Sungrass Egg by the time the ability resolves.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Trigon of Corruption. The "that artifact" that the trigger on the stack refers to is the one that Curse Artifact was attached to as the ability triggered.
judge_reason: The reference says the artifact referenced is the one Curse Artifact was attached to when the ability triggered (Trigon of Corruption), while the candidate says it updates to whatever it's attached to when the ability resolves (Sungrass Egg), so they reach opposite conclusions.

question: Alex casts [Brainstorm] using the ability of [Jace, Telepath Unbound]. Nina casts [Memory Lapse] and counters Brainstorm. Where does Brainstorm go?
answer:
Brainstorm is exiled, not put on top of Alex's library. When Nina's Memory Lapse counters Brainstorm, it is removed from the stack as a countered spell [701.6a]. Normally a countered spell goes to its owner's graveyard [404.1], but two replacement effects are competing to change that destination here: Memory Lapse's own text ("put it on top of its owner's library instead of into that player's graveyard") and Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability, which put Brainstorm on the stack from Alex's graveyard and stipulates "If that spell would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead." The Memory Lapse rulings tell us exactly how this kind of clash resolves: Memory Lapse's self-replacement effect normally intercepts the graveyard-bound event first, but when the spell was set up to go to exile instead of the graveyard because of the way it was cast (the ruling specifically cites flashback, which uses the same 'would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead' wording that Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability uses), that exile replacement wins and the spell ends up in exile instead of the library [Memory Lapse ruling #0]. Since Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability uses that identical pattern, Brainstorm's own countered-spell destination is overridden the same way: it goes to exile rather than to the top of Alex's library. Note that Nina, as the Memory Lapse's controller, doesn't get any say here beyond having countered the spell — the actual final zone is dictated by Jace, Telepath Unbound's replacement effect on Brainstorm itself. Also, per rule 733.1/701.6b there's no refund of the mana Alex spent casting Brainstorm regardless of where it ends up. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table, since it turns purely on replacement-effect interaction on a single spell rather than on turn order or opponent choices.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Alex's library.

Two replacement effects are trying to replace the same event. Since Memory Lapse's effect is a self-replacement effect, it applies first. Once it's applied, Brainstorm is moving to the library and Jace, Telepath Unbound's effect no longer applies.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Brainstorm is exiled due to Jace's replacement effect winning, whereas the reference states Memory Lapse's self-replacement applies first and Brainstorm goes to Alex's library, so the final rulings conflict.

question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
answer:
The three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave through the whole process, and that fact lets Nixon tell the two manifested creatures apart even though Ghastly Conscription tries to disguise them.

Walking through it: Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from the target graveyard face down, shuffles that face-down pile, then manifests each card (put onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature, per the card's own text). That's two zone changes for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave: graveyard → exile, and exile → battlefield. Skullbriar's own ability reads 'Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library.' Neither of those two moves is to a hand or a library, so under that ability the +1/+1 counters travel with the card each time, arriving on the battlefield already in place when it's manifested [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. Ruling #6 confirms that when a card carrying Skullbriar's counter-retention text leaves the battlefield (or, as here, changes zones with that text active) the counters remain on it, and ruling #4 confirms it becomes a brand-new object each time but the counters themselves still stick around unless the card goes to a hand or library.

Once it lands on the battlefield as a manifested permanent, though, it's face down, and rule [708.2a] says a face-down permanent (absent other instructions) is 'a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost' — manifest doesn't grant it any different base characteristics. So the object no longer has Skullbriar's name or its counter ability once face down; it's just a nameless 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters already sitting on it, making it a 5/5 face-down creature. The Southern Elephant, by contrast, is manifested as a plain 2/2 face-down creature with no counters.

Because of that size difference, Nixon (and anyone watching) can immediately tell the two manifested creatures apart: the 5/5 (2/2 plus three +1/+1 counters) is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, and the 2/2 with no counters is Southern Elephant. Ghastly Conscription's shuffle is meant to hide which pile member is which [Ghastly Conscription ruling #0], but rule [708.6] requires a player to be able to easily differentiate their own face-down permanents at all times, and here the counters themselves are exactly such a distinguishing feature — so the shuffle doesn't actually conceal Skullbriar's identity from its own controller.

This assumes the graveyard-to-exile and exile-to-battlefield movements both occur as part of Ghastly Conscription's resolution with no player having priority to remove the counters in between (there's no chance to respond to a resolving spell's internal instructions), so the counters have no opportunity to be stripped off along the way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nixon will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Southern Elephant.
judge_reason: The candidate says the +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar after it becomes a face-down manifested permanent, but the reference states the counters cease to exist once it enters the battlefield face down (even though Nixon can still deduce which is which).

question: Asa casts [Chatterstorm]. In response, Nico casts [Gather Specimens]. After everything resolves, Asa activates the second ability of [Homeward Path]. Who gains control of the token?
answer:
Nico ends up controlling the token both before and after Homeward Path is activated — activating Homeward Path doesn't change anything here. Here's why: Chatterstorm creates a 1/1 green Squirrel creature token. Normally, per rule [111.2], the player who creates a token is its owner, and the token enters the battlefield under that player's control — that would be Asa. However, Nico's Gather Specimens is already resolved and its replacement effect is active for the rest of the turn: "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Since the Squirrel token would enter under Asa's control, and Asa is Nico's opponent, Gather Specimens replaces that and the token enters the battlefield under Nico's control instead. Because the token's actual owner is defined by whose control it entered under (as clarified by [Homeward Path ruling #1], "The owner of a token is the player under whose control the token was put onto the battlefield"), Nico is both the owner and the controller of the Squirrel token. When Asa later activates Homeward Path's second ability, "Each player gains control of all creatures they own," the Squirrel token is owned by Nico, so this ability causes Nico to gain control of it — which Nico already has. Asa's own creatures (if any) would return to Asa, but the Squirrel token stays with Nico throughout. This scenario is only defined for two players (Asa and Nico); no multiplayer-specific rule was given here, so if a third player's creatures were also on the battlefield, Homeward Path would still just return each player's own creatures to them per its plain text, but I don't have multiplayer-specific rules text to note any variation beyond that.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Asa does. Tokens are owned by the player that created them. Asa still created the token, regardless of under whose control it entered the battlefield.
judge_reason: The candidate incorrectly states Nico owns the token due to Gather Specimens and thus keeps control, contradicting the correct ruling that the token is owned by its creator Asa and so Asa gains control via Homeward Path.

question: Neil controls [Willow Elf] enchanted with [Felidar Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Anger of the Gods]. What happens?
answer:
Willow Elf (a 1/1) is dealt 3 damage by Anger of the Gods, which is lethal, so as a state-based action Willow Elf would be destroyed. At that moment two replacement effects are competing to modify what happens to Willow Elf: Felidar Umbra's umbra armor ability ("If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura") and Anger of the Gods' own replacement ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead"). Because both effects are trying to modify the same event affecting the same object, rule 616.1e/616.1f says Neil — as the controller of Willow Elf, the affected permanent — chooses which one to apply first, and once one is applied, the other is checked again and may no longer be applicable.

If Neil applies Felidar Umbra's umbra armor first: Willow Elf is never actually destroyed. Instead, all damage is removed from Willow Elf and Felidar Umbra itself is destroyed (put into Neil's graveyard) [702.89a, Felidar Umbra ruling #3, Felidar Umbra ruling #4]. Because Willow Elf never dies, Anger of the Gods' "exile instead of dying" clause has nothing left to modify and does nothing [Anger of the Gods ruling #0, 615.1... effectively 616.1f's rule that an already-resolved replacement leaves the other one moot]. Willow Elf survives on the battlefield, undamaged, with no Aura attached.

If Neil instead applies Anger of the Gods' replacement first: Willow Elf's would-be death (going to the graveyard) is replaced with exile instead [Anger of the Gods ruling #0]. Since Willow Elf was never destroyed in the graveyard-bound sense that umbra armor cares about, umbra armor's replacement no longer has anything to apply to, so Felidar Umbra is not saved by that ability. Willow Elf is exiled instead of dying. (What then happens to Felidar Umbra, now enchanting nothing, isn't covered by any rule given here, so I can't state its exact fate with a citation — only that Willow Elf itself ends up in exile under this branch.)

Either way, this is a single choice made by Willow Elf's controller (Neil); since only one player's permanent is involved, this works the same whether the game has two players or more than two — the APNAP ordering rule (101.4) only matters when multiple players must make such choices simultaneously, which isn't the case here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Felidar Umbra is destroyed and moves to the graveyard. Willow Elf remains on the battlefield. If it would die later in the turn, it'll be exiled instead. Felidar Umbra's effect replaces the "destroy" event while Anger of the Gods's effect replaces the "die" event, so Felidar Umbra has to be applied first.
judge_reason: The candidate says the creature's controller can choose which replacement applies (allowing either survival or exile), while the reference concludes Felidar Umbra must apply first so Willow Elf survives, so the final rulings conflict.

question: Noah controls [Compost]. Ainsley controls [Dune Beetle] and a token that was created as a copy of [Bogstomper]. Ainsley casts [Soulscour]. How many times does Compost trigger?
answer:
Compost triggers exactly once. Compost's trigger condition is "Whenever a black card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere." When Ainsley's Soulscour resolves, it destroys all nonartifact permanents at once, which is a single event, but per rule [603.2c] a triggered ability "can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences" — so Compost checks each qualifying occurrence within that mass-destruction event separately. Ainsley controls two nonartifact permanents that die simultaneously: Dune Beetle and a token that was created as a copy of Bogstomper.

Dune Beetle is an actual black card, so its being put into Ainsley's graveyard is one qualifying occurrence, and Compost triggers for it.

The token copy of Bogstomper, however, is not a card at all — it's a token. The rules consistently distinguish "permanent" from "permanent card" (see the terminology used in [700.11], which specifically talks about "permanent cards" being put into a graveyard as distinct from permanents generally), reflecting that tokens are permanents but are not cards. Compost's trigger explicitly requires a black *card* to be put into the graveyard, not merely a black permanent. Since the Bogstomper token isn't a card, its death (it briefly hits the graveyard and then ceases to exist as a state-based action) doesn't satisfy Compost's trigger condition, so it does not generate a second trigger.

So out of the two black permanents Ainsley loses to Soulscour, only Dune Beetle actually causes Compost to trigger, giving Noah one opportunity to draw a card. This holds whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, since Compost only cares about cards going to "an opponent's" graveyard, and Ainsley is an opponent of Noah either way; the number of other players at the table doesn't change this count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
0. Soulscour destroys all permanents simultaneously. Compost's trigger checks immediately after the event in question to see if it should trigger. However by that time Compost is in the graveyard, and its ability doesn't function there.

(Compost doesn't fit the "leaves-the-battlefield" trigger exception because it's a "from anywhere" trigger.)
judge_reason: The candidate says Compost triggers once (for Dune Beetle), but the reference says it triggers zero times because Compost is in the graveyard after Soulscour's mass destruction and its ability can't function there, so the conclusions differ.

question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Because Albert is controlling Brielle during Brielle's turn (per Worst Fears), rule [723.4] applies: any information about an object in the game that would be visible to the player being controlled (Brielle) is visible to both Brielle and the player controlling her (Albert). The identity of the opponent secretly chosen when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield is information about an object in the game (Stalking Leonin) that Brielle, as its controller, already knows. Since that information is visible to Brielle, it becomes visible to Albert as well while he controls her.

Note that this only covers information about game objects — if Stalking Leonin's chosen opponent had instead been recorded via some off-game method involving cards outside the game, rule [723.4] specifies that information about cards outside the game is visible only to the controlled player, not the controller. But the Stalking Leonin ruling [Stalking Leonin ruling #0] confirms the secret choice can be tracked by writing the name on paper kept with the card, which is information tied to the permanent (an in-game object), so it falls under the first sentence of [723.4] and is shared with Albert.

This also holds regardless of whether this is a two-player or multiplayer game, since [723.4] doesn't depend on player count — it's purely about what information the controlled player can see, which Albert then also sees.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Brielle. Albert can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Albert can see the secret choice (misapplying rule 723.4 and treating the selection as visible), whereas the reference states the choice was made when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield and remains hidden, so the conclusions conflict.

question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx will enter the battlefield with only 1 +1/+1 counter, not 2 -- Primal Vigor's doubling effect does not apply here.

Rescuer Sphinx's ability reads: "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Per [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0], the choice of what to return is made while Rescuer Sphinx is entering the battlefield, and "no player may take actions between the time you choose which permanent to return and the time Rescuer Sphinx is on the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter." Angel of Sanctions ruling #4 directly addresses this exact scenario: if Angel of Sanctions's owner leaves the game, the exiled card still returns to the battlefield, because the returning effect isn't an ability on the stack and so isn't wiped out along with the leaving player's stack objects under rule [800.4a]. So even though Bobbie (the owner) is leaving the game and taking Angel of Sanctions with them, Rotted Hystrix still pops back onto the battlefield under Conrad's control (its owner) right as Angel of Sanctions leaves the game.

Meanwhile, Alana's Lava Axe has already resolved and finishes doing its job (dealing the 5 damage that put Bobbie's life at -4); Lava Axe itself doesn't care what happens to Bobbie afterward. The game then continues between Conrad and Alana under rule [800.4], since multiplayer games can continue after a player leaves.

One timing note: I'm assuming Bobbie's loss (and thus leaving the game) is processed as a state-based action after Lava Axe fully resolves, which is the normal sequencing — if instead something checked life totals mid-resolution that wouldn't change the outcome here, since Lava Axe has only one effect (5 damage) and nothing else depends on Bobbie's life total before the spell finishes resolving.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: All objects owned by Bobbie leave the game. However the game treats phased-out permanents as nonexistent, and does not see the leaves-the-battlefield event happen. Rotted Hystrix will not return to the battlefield.
