question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
answer:
No. Nico's Hallow will not prevent combat damage dealt later when Keldon Champion attacks. Hallow reads "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn," and it can only target an object that is currently a spell — here, the Keldon Champion creature spell on the stack (rule 117.7 confirms Hallow, cast in response, resolves first). But under rule 400.7a, when the Keldon Champion spell resolves it becomes a new object (the Keldon Champion permanent) with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence as a spell. The only exceptions to that rule are effects that change the characteristics or controller of the permanent (rule 400.7a, rule 112.4) — a damage-prevention effect is neither of those, so it does not carry over to the permanent. Once Keldon Champion is a permanent, any damage it deals (its 'enters the battlefield' triggered ability dealing 3 damage, or its combat damage when it attacks) is dealt by that permanent/its ability, not by 'the spell' Hallow targeted. In fact, a creature spell itself never deals damage as it resolves — it just enters the battlefield — so Hallow's prevention effect ends up with nothing to prevent from the spell, and it has no bearing on the creature's later combat damage. So when Keldon Champion attacks, its combat damage goes through normally and is not prevented by Hallow. (This same reasoning also means the 3 damage from Keldon Champion's enters-the-battlefield trigger is not prevented by Hallow, for the same reason — that damage is dealt by a triggered ability of the permanent, not by 'the spell.')

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Yes. Effects that apply to damage from a spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Hallow will not prevent the creature's later damage, which directly contradicts the reference ruling that the prevention effect on the spell continues to apply to the damage dealt by the permanent it becomes.

question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
answer:
No. Suspending Shivan Meteor is a special action, not casting a spell, so it can't satisfy Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability, which only lets Amelia cast an instant or sorcery spell from her hand without paying its mana cost. Under rule [116.2f], exiling a card using suspend is a special action available any time a player has priority (and only if they could begin to cast it) — it explicitly does not use the stack and is not the act of casting. Rule [702.62a] confirms suspend's first ability lets you 'exile it' rather than cast it. Shivan Meteor's own ruling reinforces this: 'Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting that card. This action doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to' (Shivan Meteor ruling #3). Wildfire Eternal's second ability specifically grants permission to *cast* a spell for free as the trigger resolves — per Wildfire Eternal ruling #1, 'you must cast a spell at that time if you wish to cast one without paying its mana cost.' Since suspending Shivan Meteor is not casting it, choosing to suspend it does not fulfill that ability. Additionally, rule [601.2b] states a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell — Wildfire Eternal's 'cast without paying its mana cost' is itself a cost-substitution, and it can't be combined with Shivan Meteor's Suspend 2—{1}{R}{R} alternative cost even if suspend did involve casting (which it doesn't). So as Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves, Amelia's only options are to cast Shivan Meteor outright for free (dealing 13 damage to a target creature) or decline to cast anything; she cannot use this trigger to suspend it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Shivan Meteor could be cast from Amelia's hand. Normally that's only when Amelia has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)
judge_reason: The candidate forbids using suspend during Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability, which contradicts the reference ruling that suspend is a special action available while that trigger resolves and thus can be taken then.

question: Ariel controls [Soul Seizer] (back face [Ghastly Haunting])which has been mutated with [Everquill Phoenix]. Everquill Phoenix is the top component. Naomi controls [Axegrinder Giant]. Ariel then attacks Naomi with the merged permanent. Naomi declared no blockers and the merged permanent deals damage to Naomi. What happens when the transformation trigger resolves if Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent and targets Axegrinder Giant?
answer:
When Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent (Soul Seizer/Ghastly Haunting merged with Everquill Phoenix) and targets Axegrinder Giant, the result is: Soul Seizer's component turns face up as Ghastly Haunting, Everquill Phoenix stays as it is, and the whole merged permanent becomes attached to Axegrinder Giant while remaining a creature (not an Enchantment) — and because the Ghastly Haunting ability is now part of the merged permanent, Ariel gains control of Axegrinder Giant.

Here's why. A mutated permanent (the Everquill Phoenix / Soul Seizer merge) is a single permanent represented by more than one card, with 'all abilities of each card and token that represents it,' but its other characteristics (power, toughness, card types, etc.) are derived only from the topmost card — here, Everquill Phoenix [702.140e]. Soul Seizer's triggered ability ('When this creature deals combat damage to a player, you may transform it. If you do, attach it to target creature that player controls') is one of the abilities the merged permanent has, since it comes from the Soul Seizer/Ghastly Haunting component. You chose the target (Axegrinder Giant) when the ability triggered, and you choose whether to transform when the ability resolves [Soul Seizer // Ghastly Haunting ruling #0].

Because Soul Seizer is a double-faced card and is a component of this merged permanent, transforming the merged permanent causes that component to turn so its Ghastly Haunting face is up; Everquill Phoenix, not being double-faced, is unaffected and can't itself transform [730.2i, 712.9]. Transforming is not the same action as an object leaving the battlefield or becoming a new object — the merged permanent doesn't leave the battlefield, and any ongoing effects on it (e.g., it's still attacking, still has any counters, etc.) continue to apply [712.18, 701.27g, 701.27b].

However, since the merged permanent's 'other characteristics' still come from the topmost card, Everquill Phoenix, the merged permanent remains a 4/4 flying Creature — Phoenix; it does NOT become an Enchantment — Aura just because its Ghastly Haunting face turned up [702.140e]. What does carry over is the ability text: the merged permanent now has Ghastly Haunting's ability, 'You control enchanted creature,' as one of the abilities granted by that component [702.140e], and the resolving trigger instructs you to attach it to Axegrinder Giant. So the merged permanent becomes attached to Axegrinder Giant (functioning like an Aura for attachment purposes even though it's still a creature by type), and because it's now 'enchanting' Axegrinder Giant, its 'You control enchanted creature' ability gives Ariel control of Axegrinder Giant.

Note: this is a two-player scenario as described (Ariel attacking Naomi); nothing here depends on multiplayer-specific rules, but with more than two players the same mechanics for merging, transforming, and control-changing would apply per player interactions, only the choice of defending player/opponents would differ, which isn't at issue here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
The component that consists of Soul Seizer is transformed. The merged permanent is still a creature. It is not attached to anything. The merged permanent has the abilities in the text box of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half.

When Ariel chooses to transform the merged permanent, all double-faced components are transformed. The merged permanent now has the abilities of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half. ([702.140e]) The merged permanent is still a creature as Everquill Phoenix is still the topmost card. When the transformation trigger tries to attach the merged permanent to Axegrinder Giant, it can't attach because the merged permanent is still a creature. It remains on the battlefield because the state-based action that puts auras not attached to anything into the graveyard is looking for the "Aura" subtype, not the "Enchant" keyword.
judge_reason: The candidate incorrectly says the merged permanent can attach and gain control of Axegrinder Giant, whereas the correct ruling is the transformed component gains the back-face abilities but the merged permanent remains a creature and cannot attach as an Aura, so it does not become attached or gain control.

question: Nadia has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Ashley controls a [Peacewalker Colossus] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts a [Clever Impersonator], choosing to have it copy Peacewalker Colossus. What happens?
answer:
Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield under Ashley's control as a copy of Peacewalker Colossus — an Artifact — Vehicle, 6/6, with "Crew 4" and "{1}{W}: Another target Vehicle you control becomes an artifact creature until end of turn." It does NOT enter as a creature, so Nadia's Gather Specimens never applies, and there is no control-swap.

Here's why: Peacewalker Colossus's printed type line is Artifact — Vehicle, not Artifact Creature — Vehicle. The fact that Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus is *currently* a creature is because of a temporary, non-copy effect (its own {1}{W} ability making it a creature until end of turn, or crewing). Clever Impersonator ruling #2 explicitly states that Clever Impersonator "copies exactly what is printed on the chosen permanent... it doesn't copy any non-copy effects that have changed that permanent's power, toughness, types, color, abilities, or so on." This matches rule [707.2], which says a copy uses the copiable values derived from the printed text, and that "other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects)... are not copied."

Under rule [707.5], an object that enters the battlefield as a copy of another object becomes that copy as it enters — it doesn't enter first and then transform. So as Clever Impersonator enters, it is already an Artifact — Vehicle, 6/6, not a creature (the crew/activated 'becomes a creature' effect on Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus is a separate, non-copied effect that doesn't carry over per rule [707.3] and the ruling above).

Nadia's Gather Specimens reads, "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Because Clever Impersonator is entering as a noncreature Vehicle (not a creature), the trigger condition "a creature would enter" is never met, so Gather Specimens simply does nothing here — Ashley keeps Clever Impersonator, which is a 6/6 Artifact — Vehicle named Peacewalker Colossus that isn't currently a creature (it could later become one via its own {1}{W} ability targeting another Vehicle it doesn't have, or by being crewed, since it retains the Crew 4 ability as part of its copied text).

This analysis assumes a standard two-player game between Nadia and Ashley; the outcome (no creature enters, so Gather Specimens is irrelevant) would be the same at a multiplayer table too, since the trigger condition for Gather Specimens still requires an actual creature to be entering.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: This can't happen as described. As Clever Impersonator begins to resolve, Nadia gains control of it before any other choices are made. Nadia will make the choice of what to copy as it enters the battlefield.
judge_reason: The candidate says the Impersonator enters under Ashley's control (so Gather Specimens doesn't apply), while the reference says Nadia gains control as it enters and gets to choose what it copies.

question: Aubrey controls a [Gaea's Liege], [Rhonas the Indomitable], and 1 [Forest]. Noel controls 5 Forest. Can Aubrey attack with the Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable?
answer:
Yes. Aubrey can declare both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable as attackers this combat, because once Gaea's Liege is declared an attacker its power/toughness immediately becomes 5/5 (equal to the number of Forests Noel, the defending player, controls), which satisfies Rhonas the Indomitable's attack restriction.

Here's the sequencing: under [508.1a], the active player (Aubrey) first chooses which creatures will attack – she can choose both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable, since both are untapped and have been under her control since the turn began. The act of being declared an attacker is what makes a creature 'attacking' (tapping is merely a consequence of that declaration, per [508.1f], not a prerequisite for the 'attacking' state). Gaea's Liege's own text overrides the default characteristics rule here: 'As long as Gaea's Liege is attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls.' Since Noel controls 5 Forests, as soon as Gaea's Liege is declared as an attacker it becomes 5/5.

Next, under [508.1c], the game checks restrictions on the chosen attackers. Rhonas the Indomitable's printed text says 'Rhonas can't attack or block unless you control another creature with power 4 or greater.' At this point in the declare-attackers turn-based action, Gaea's Liege is already an attacking 5/5, so Aubrey does control another creature with power 4 or greater, satisfying Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction. [Rhonas the Indomitable ruling #1] confirms that the other power-4-or-greater creature does not itself need to be attacking to satisfy this clause — but here Gaea's Liege only reaches power 4+ because it is attacking (its non-attacking power/toughness would just be 1, from Aubrey's single Forest), so both creatures need to be declared as attackers together for this to work.

If instead Aubrey tried to attack with only Rhonas the Indomitable while leaving Gaea's Liege back, Gaea's Liege would remain at 1/1 (based on Aubrey's own 1 Forest), and Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction would not be satisfied, making that attack illegal under [508.1c] (the whole declaration would be undone per [733.1]). But attacking with both together is legal.

Note: this analysis assumes normal two-player rules as presented; if this is a multiplayer game, Aubrey would still need to choose which defending player each attacker is attacking, but the mechanics of Gaea's Liege's and Rhonas the Indomitable's restrictions work the same way relative to whichever player is being attacked.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: No. All creatures are declared as attackers at the same time. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".
judge_reason: The candidate concludes both creatures can attack, contradicting the reference which states restrictions are checked before creatures become attacking so Rhonas' requirement would not be met.

question: Ariyah casts [Stonewood Invocation] targeting [Skeletal Crocodile], and then attacks with the Skeletal Crocodile. Noah blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Phyresis] and indestructible due to their [Valorous Stance]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
By the end of the turn, Baron Sengir survives (it's not destroyed despite taking lethal combat damage), and Skeletal Crocodile is left with five permanent -1/-1 counters on it once the Stonewood Invocation pump wears off — whether that actually finishes off Skeletal Crocodile is the one piece I can't confirm from the rules given to me (see the note at the end).

Step by step:

1) Combat damage is dealt simultaneously. Skeletal Crocodile (pumped to 10/6 by Stonewood Invocation's +5/+5) has no infect, so its 10 damage to Baron Sengir is marked normally [302.7], [120.6]. Baron Sengir is a 5/5, so 10 marked damage is well over its toughness — normally lethal — but Baron Sengir has indestructible from Valorous Stance, so it "can't be destroyed" and "ignore[s] the state-based action that checks for lethal damage" [702.12b], [704.5g]. Baron Sengir survives the combat step with 10 damage marked on it but is not destroyed.

2) Baron Sengir has infect (from Phyresis), so its 5 combat damage to Skeletal Crocodile is never marked as damage. Instead, Noah (Baron Sengir's controller) puts five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile [702.90c], [120.3d], [702.90e]. Skeletal Crocodile's shroud (from Stonewood Invocation) only stops it from being *targeted* by spells/abilities — it does nothing to prevent combat damage or the resulting counters, so this happens normally. During combat, Skeletal Crocodile is 10/6 minus five -1/-1 counters = 5/1, which is still alive (toughness 1 > 0, and it has no marked damage triggering the lethal-damage SBA).

3) At the cleanup step, two things happen simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all "until end of turn" effects end [514.2]. This removes Baron Sengir's 10 marked damage (so no lethal-damage check applies to it at all after this point) and ends both Stonewood Invocation's +5/+5-and-shroud and Valorous Stance's indestructible. Phyresis is a permanently-attached Aura, not an "until end of turn" effect, so Baron Sengir keeps infect going forward.

4) The five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile are counters, not damage, so cleanup does *not* remove them [514.2 only removes damage and "until end of turn" effects; counters persist]. Once the +5/+5 wears off, Skeletal Crocodile reverts to its base 5/1 with five -1/-1 counters still on it, making it a 0/-4.

Here's the gap: whether a creature with 0-or-less toughness is actually put into the graveyard is normally a state-based action, and Baron Sengir's own triggered ability ("Whenever a creature dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn dies, put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir") would matter if Skeletal Crocodile does die this turn — but the specific state-based action for 0-or-less toughness creatures, and the cleanup-step rule about re-checking state-based actions/triggers, were not among the rules provided to me. So I can't cite a rule confirming Skeletal Crocodile is actually put into the graveyard or that Baron Sengir gets its +2/+2 counter, even though the counters clearly drop its toughness below 1.

Summary of what's certain: Baron Sengir ends the turn undamaged (marked damage cleared) and keeps infect permanently; Skeletal Crocodile ends the turn back at its base size plus five permanent -1/-1 counters (net 0/-4 stats), with its actual survival/death not confirmable from the rules given here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: The effect from Stonewood Invocation wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile remain. Skeletal Crocodile dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.
judge_reason: The candidate fails to conclude that Skeletal Crocodile dies when the pump ends and therefore misses that Baron Sengir's death-trigger occurs, which disagrees with the reference ruling.

question: Alejandra owns a face-down [Progenitus] in exile. Nicolas uses [Ruin Processor] to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard. Where does Progenitus move to?
answer:
Progenitus does not end up in Alejandra's graveyard at all. Progenitus's own printed replacement effect says, "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." Ruin Processor's ability tries to put the exiled Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard, but that movement is a case of a card being 'put into a graveyard,' so Progenitus's replacement effect intercepts it: Progenitus is revealed (even though it was exiled face down) and is shuffled into Alejandra's library instead of going to her graveyard. Nicolas still gets to choose whether to gain 5 life as part of Ruin Processor's ability, since the ability's instruction to 'put a card... into that player's graveyard' is what's being replaced — the act of attempting it is what triggers Progenitus's replacement, similar to how Ruin Processor ruling #1 describes a replacement effect that changes where a card ends up when something tries to put it into a graveyard from exile. Progenitus's card text overrides the general outcome you'd otherwise expect from Ruin Processor's ability, since a card's own printed rules text always wins over how a general effect would otherwise apply. This is a two-player scenario (Nicolas and Alejandra), and nothing here depends on player count, so the same result would hold at a multiplayer table as well.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: The graveyard. Replacement effects must exist before the event in question in order to affect it. Progenitus has no abilities in exile, so there is no replacement effect that would apply to it moving to the graveyard.
judge_reason: The candidate incorrectly applies Progenitus's replacement effect while it's in exile (face-down), claiming it shuffles into the library instead of going to the graveyard, which contradicts the reference ruling that it has no replacement effect in exile.

question: Aurora controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Snow-Covered Forest. Can Aurora attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
No — Aurora cannot legally declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico while Reverence is on the battlefield, because the act of declaring it attacking causes its own power to drop low enough to trigger Reverence's restriction.

Here's why: Gaea's Liege's power/toughness are characteristic-defining. While it is *not* attacking, it's a */* equal to the number of Forests Aurora controls (3 Snow-Covered Forests, since Snow-Covered Forest has the basic land type Forest), making it a 3/3. But the moment Aurora chooses to declare it as an attacker, it becomes an 'attacking' creature per the declare-attackers process (rule 508.1), and Gaea's Liege's ability then reads 'its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls.' Nico, the defending player, controls only 1 Snow-Covered Forest, so as soon as Gaea's Liege becomes an attacking creature it is a 1/1.

Reverence reads 'Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you' — this is a Restriction (see the Restriction definition and rules 508.1c/509.1b). Restrictions on attacking are checked during the declare-attackers step: the active player checks each creature they control for restrictions, and if any restriction is being disobeyed, the whole declaration of attackers is illegal (rule 508.1c). Since Gaea's Liege's power becomes 1 (≤2) the instant it's declared attacking Nico, declaring it as an attacker against Nico violates Reverence's restriction, making the attack declaration illegal. If Aurora tried to do this, the game would treat it as an illegal action and roll back to before the declaration (rule 733.1).

This answer assumes a two-player game between Aurora and Nico, since Nico is the only opponent mentioned. If this were a multiplayer game and Aurora had other opponents within her range of influence (rule 801.3), Gaea's Liege could still be declared attacking one of those other opponents (or their planeswalkers/battles) instead, where its power/toughness would be based on that other defending player's Forests, and Reverence — which only restricts attacks against Nico specifically — would not apply to those attacks (rule 802.3a: restrictions that apply to attacking a specific player only apply to creatures attacking that player).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Yes. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".
judge_reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion, incorrectly claiming the Liege's power changes upon declaration and is barred by Reverence, while the reference correctly states restrictions are checked before a creature becomes attacking so the Liege is a 3/3 and may attack.

question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
answer:
No. Time Vault's ability only lets Autumn skip a turn *if Time Vault is tapped* at the moment that turn would begin, and skipping a turn with Time Vault automatically untaps it. So Autumn can use Time Vault to skip at most one of the two extra turns from Time Stretch, not both.

Here's the sequence: Time Stretch ("Target player takes two extra turns after this one") gives Autumn two extra turns, added one at a time directly after the current turn [500.7]. When the first of those extra turns would begin, if Time Vault is tapped, Autumn may choose to skip that turn instead — and if they do, Time Vault untaps immediately as part of that choice (Time Vault's own text: "If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact"; confirmed by [Time Vault ruling #1], which notes the choice is made as the turn would begin, only while Time Vault is tapped, and Time Vault untaps before anything else happens next). Skipping a turn is a replacement effect [614.10a][614.10b][500.11] that simply causes the game to proceed as though that turn never happened.

Because Time Vault untaps the moment the first extra turn is skipped, it is no longer tapped when the second extra turn from Time Stretch would begin. Time Vault's skip ability only triggers off the artifact being tapped at that specific moment, so the condition isn't met for the second turn, and Autumn has no way to skip it with Time Vault (they'd need to tap it again first, e.g. by using its "{T}: Take an extra turn after this one" ability, but that generates yet another extra turn rather than letting them skip the pending one). So at most one of the two Time Stretch extra turns can be skipped this way, never both.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Yes. As their turn ends, they can apply Time Vault's replacement effect, which means the next turn gets skipped and Time Vault gets untapped as part of the next turn that actually happens. Then, since it's still tapped as Autumn's turn is ending, they can choose to skip the next turn again.
judge_reason: The candidate concludes Autumn can skip at most one of Time Stretch's extra turns with Time Vault, while the reference says they can skip both, so the final rulings conflict.
